item.message: `[features].memory_tool` is deprecated. Use `[features].memories` instead. (Enable it with `--enable memories` or `[features].memories` in config.toml. See https://developers.openai.com/codex/config-basic#feature-flags for details.)

item.text:
1. **Section 2(1)(A) — “artificial intelligence model” is undefined.** The bill does not specify what qualifies as AI or as a distinct model, allowing developers to characterize a system as conventional software, a collection of components, or something other than a “model.”

2. **Section 2(1)(A) — The compute threshold lacks a measurement methodology.** “Integer or floating-point operations” does not address precision, sparsity, skipped operations, failed runs, data preprocessing, reinforcement learning, fine-tuning, synthetic-data generation, or other post-training computation, making the threshold difficult to calculate or audit consistently.

3. **Section 2(1)(A) — Exactly \(10^{26}\) operations are excluded.** Because the threshold is “greater than” rather than “equal to or greater than,” a model trained using exactly \(10^{26}\) operations is not covered.

4. **Section 2(1)(A) — “Single training run” invites artificial partitioning.** A company could divide training among nominally separate runs, checkpoints, subsidiaries, facilities, or successive fine-tunes while producing a model that cumulatively exceeds the threshold.

5. **Section 2(1)(A) — Distributed and component-based systems can evade the threshold.** The bill does not aggregate computation across multiple models, agents, mixture-of-experts components, or models combined through scaffolding, so a powerful system could be assembled entirely from nominally subthreshold models.

6. **Section 2(1)(A) — The threshold is static and may rapidly become obsolete.** It cannot be adjusted for algorithmic improvements, hardware changes, or evidence that dangerous capabilities arise below \(10^{26}\) operations.

7. **Section 2(1)(A) — Coverage may arise only after the prohibited training has occurred.** A model does not clearly become “trained using” more than the threshold until the run crosses it, creating uncertainty about when the violation begins and whether preparatory computation is prohibited.

8. **Section 2(1)(B) — The capability standard is highly vague.** “Substantially exceeding human performance,” “most,” and “cognitive tasks” lack benchmarks, comparison populations, domains, time horizons, and testing conditions, creating both an avoidance opportunity and a vagueness challenge.

9. **Section 2(1)(B) — Coverage depends entirely on an unspecified Secretary’s determination.** The bill neither identifies which Secretary nor supplies procedures, deadlines, evidentiary standards, testing authority, notice rules, or emergency authority for making a determination; a dangerous system may remain lawful until the determination is completed.

10. **Section 2(1)(B) — The Secretary cannot clearly designate categories or anticipated systems.** The provision appears to require a system-specific determination after capabilities are demonstrated, rather than permitting rules covering model families, successors, substantially similar systems, or systems reasonably expected to meet the standard.

11. **Section 2(1) — “Model” and “system” are used inconsistently.** Paragraph (A) covers a model while paragraph (B) covers a system, leaving uncertainty about whether applications, agents, model ensembles, fine-tunes, and systems incorporating a covered model inherit covered status.

12. **Section 2(2) — “U.S. person” omits many important persons and entities.** It excludes permanent residents and other U.S. residents, partnerships, trusts, unincorporated associations, federally or territorially organized corporations, governmental entities, and potentially limited liability companies not treated as corporations.

13. **Section 2(2) — Corporate restructuring offers an easy evasion route.** A U.S. company could conduct work through a foreign-organized subsidiary or joint venture because the definition does not cover entities owned or controlled by U.S. persons.

14. **Section 2(3) — “Data center,” “operator,” and “advanced AI chip” are undefined.** Companies could dispute whether a site is a data center, whether particular accelerators count, or which landlord, cloud provider, customer, or contractor is the operator responsible for registering.

15. **Section 2(3) — The facility threshold is both narrow and easy to evade.** A facility with exactly 50,000 chips is excluded, and an operator can distribute 50,000-or-fewer chips among adjacent buildings, campuses, mobile facilities, or coordinated sites because no aggregation or anti-evasion rule applies.

16. **Section 2(3) — Chip count is a poor and static proxy for capability.** The definition ignores chip performance, interconnects, utilization, remote aggregation, and future hardware, while exempting extremely capable facilities containing fewer than 50,001 chips.

17. **Section 3(a) — “Train,” “develop,” and “deploy” are undefined.** It is unclear whether these terms cover fine-tuning, continued pretraining, reinforcement learning, distillation, modification, copying, hosting, operating, providing API access, releasing weights, or integrating a model into another product.

18. **Section 3(a) — Key enabling conduct is not prohibited.** The section does not expressly prohibit attempting, conspiring, financing, facilitating, procuring, exporting relevant technology, providing compute, transferring model weights, possessing a covered system, or knowingly assisting another person’s violation.

19. **Section 3(a) — The territorial language is ambiguous.** “Any person in the United States” could refer to the person’s physical or legal presence rather than where the conduct occurs, generating uncertainty about remote foreign actors using U.S. facilities and foreign entities with a U.S. office.

20. **Section 3(a) — There is no anti-circumvention or attribution rule.** Companies may outsource steps, allocate work among affiliates or contractors, or arrange nominal foreign control while retaining the benefit of the prohibited activity.

21. **Section 3(b) — The grandfather clause is exceptionally broad and permanent.** Any system whose “training began” before enactment is exempt, with no requirement that it already be covered, no completion deadline, and no limit on later training, fine-tuning, scaling, deployment, replication, or transfer.

22. **Section 3(b) — “Training began” is undefined and easily manufactured.** A token amount of pre-enactment training, creation of a checkpoint, or work on a claimed predecessor could be asserted as the beginning of training for a much larger future system.

23. **Section 3(b) — The exemption attaches to systems rather than specified training runs.** Companies could argue that future versions, descendants, fine-tunes, or systems sharing an architecture or checkpoint are the same preexisting “system.”

24. **Section 3(c) — The safety-evaluation exception can swallow the prohibition.** It is unlimited as to compute, capabilities, duration, actors, security, deployment, and necessity, and turns solely on the activity’s asserted “purpose,” allowing ordinary development to be relabeled as safety evaluation.

25. **Section 3(c) — No authorization or containment safeguards apply.** The exception requires no advance approval, independent protocol, least-risk means, reporting, secure facility, access controls, prohibition on capability enhancement, or destruction or government custody of the resulting model.

26. **Section 4(a) — Registration duties are incomplete.** The bill sets no registration deadline, required contents, update obligation, treatment of facilities crossing the threshold later, or duty to report ownership, customers, chips, location, and control relationships.

27. **Section 4 — The registry covers only large domestic facilities.** It does not cover smaller coordinated clusters, non-data-center compute, foreign facilities used by U.S. persons, cloud customers, chip owners, or entities arranging covered workloads.

28. **Section 4(b) — “Describing the computing workloads” is too indefinite.** Operators can submit high-level descriptions that omit customers, models, operation counts, run identifiers, purpose, duration, and links among distributed workloads.

29. **Section 4(b) — Reporting and certification rules lack basic enforcement details.** The bill does not identify the certifying individual, require certification under penalty of perjury, mandate records or retention, establish audit standards, or require prompt reporting of suspicious or threshold-crossing activity.

30. **Sections 4 and 5 — Registry violations carry no express penalty.** Section 5 penalizes only violations of section 3, so failure to register, report, certify accurately, or preserve information is not itself subject to the Act’s civil or criminal penalties.

31. **Sections 3–5 — No agency is expressly charged with administration or enforcement.** The bill supplies no rulemaking authority, investigative authority, subpoena power, inspection authority, audit access, testing authority, seizure or impoundment power, or express power to seek an injunction or halt an ongoing training run.

32. **Sections 3–5 — There is no compliance mechanism for determining compute or capabilities.** Developers need not notify the government before large runs, obtain licenses, submit evaluations, preserve technical records, or provide weights and access for testing, leaving the government dependent on voluntary disclosure or after-the-fact discovery.

33. **Section 5(a) — The civil penalty may be inadequate and inconsistently applied.** “Not more than” permits a nominal or zero penalty, provides no factors for setting it, and a $1 million daily maximum may be less than the economic value of continuing a major training run.

34. **Section 5(a) — The unit and duration of a violation are unclear.** The bill does not say whether separate systems, actors, facilities, deployments, copies, or training jobs constitute separate violations, or when a continuing violation begins and ends.

35. **Section 5(a) and Section 8 — The penalty date conflicts with the effective date.** Section 5 purports to impose liability for violations on or after enactment, while section 8 says the Act takes effect 180 days later; this creates serious notice, retroactivity, and enforceability problems.

36. **Section 5(b) — “Willfully” may make criminal cases unnecessarily difficult.** Depending on its construction, prosecutors may have to prove knowledge of the legal prohibition, particularly problematic given the bill’s vague technical terms and uncertain coverage.

37. **Section 5 — Responsibility inside organizations is unclear.** The bill does not expressly address corporate officer liability, responsible executives, agents, successor entities, parent companies, or persons who direct or knowingly permit violations.

38. **Section 5 — No express remedies address the dangerous system itself.** There is no forfeiture, disabling, deletion, secure custody, recall, access cutoff, or prohibition on retaining and exploiting a system produced through an unlawful run.

39. **Section 5 — The bill lacks limitations and savings provisions.** It specifies no limitations period and does not preserve accrued liability, pending enforcement actions, evidence, or remedies after the Act sunsets.

40. **Section 6 — The international-negotiation mandate is largely precatory.** “Shall seek to negotiate” requires neither conclusion nor ratification of an agreement, contains no milestones or reporting, and does not specify consequences if negotiations fail.

41. **Section 6 — “Equivalent” international prohibitions are undefined.** An agreement could be described as equivalent despite materially weaker thresholds, exceptions, verification, enforcement, territorial coverage, or duration.

42. **Section 7(a) — The termination standard is vague and procedurally incomplete.** “Acting on” a National Academies report and finding that systems “can be developed safely” do not specify who requests the report, when it must issue, what evidence or safety standard applies, or what the joint resolution must contain.

43. **Section 7(a) — The joint-resolution mechanism is not fully drafted.** It lacks introduction, committee, discharge, debate, amendment, and expedited-consideration procedures and does not clearly say that the resolution must be enacted through presentment to the President.

44. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b) — The two termination provisions conflict.** Section 7(a) says the prohibition remains effective until Congress makes a safety finding, but section 7(b) automatically terminates the entire Act after 10 years whether or not such a finding occurs.

45. **Section 7(b) — The automatic sunset creates a clear path for delayed development.** Companies can preserve plans, infrastructure, data, and perhaps grandfathered training until the tenth anniversary, after which every prohibition, registry duty, and enforcement authority disappears without an affirmative safety determination.

46. **Section 7(b) — Sunset consequences are unspecified.** The bill does not state whether pre-sunset violations remain prosecutable, whether civil liabilities survive, or whether records and investigations must continue, inviting abatement arguments.

47. **Section 8 — The 180-day delay permits an uncontrolled scaling window.** Companies can begin training before the prohibition takes effect and then invoke section 3(b)’s enactment-date grandfather clause, potentially exempting every project started during—or immediately before—the transition period.

48. **Act-wide — There is no severability clause.** A successful challenge to the vague capability standard, the extraterritorial application, the termination mechanism, or another central provision could increase the risk that a court invalidates more of the Act than necessary.

49. **Act-wide — There are no appropriations, staffing provisions, or implementation deadlines.** Even if Commerce is intended to administer the statute, it receives no expressly authorized resources and no deadline to establish measurement, registry, inspection, or enforcement systems.

50. **Act-wide — The bill lacks a general anti-evasion rule.** Given its sharp numerical thresholds and entity-based coverage, parties can structure transactions or technical processes to remain formally outside the language even when their purpose and effect are to produce a prohibited system.
